newsitem.title: USA: Mass. official says no immunity for tobacco firms.
newsitem.headline: Mass. official says no immunity for tobacco firms.

text.p: The 24 attorneys general from U.S. states that have filed suits against the tobacco firms will not agree to blanket immunity from future lawsuits as a condition of a potential settlement, Massachustts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger said on Tuesday.
The attorneys general "are united on the issue of immunity," said Harshbarger, who heads the National Association of Attorneys General.
"There is no blanket immunity at all," he said. "Blanket immunity is non-negotiable for us. It's not going to happen."
Harshbarger did say in a telephone interview he was willing to discuss "creative ways of approaching civil liabilities for past conduct and future conduct" with the tobacco companies.
Harshbarger said May 5 had been set as a tentative date for the next round of talks between negotiators for the attorneys general and the tobacco companies.

"We're not going to cut off access (to the courts) to victims," Harshbarger said. "We'll see if they want predictablity or immunity. (And if it is immunity) we're not going to talk long on that issue."

Earlier Tuesday, Texas Attorney General Dan Morales told reporters in Austin that he was willing to listen to proposals granting tobacco firms limited immunity for past alleged misdeeds, but not the future.

News reports have said the tobacco industry in settlement talks with anti-smoking groups, has proposed putting up to $300 billion over 25 years into a fund to reimburse states for Medicaid costs linked to smoking. In return, the cigarette makers would reportedly ask for broad protection from lawsuits.

Morales said the $300 billion sum "is not sufficient" for settlement, while Harshbarger said, "The reality is that money has never been raised by us as yet. It will have to be a substantial amount, but money isn't the issue. Youth access to tobacco and public health issues are the prime concerns."
Harshbarger said the 24 attorneys general were united in their strategy and that their negotiating team will be meeting over the next three or four days to hammer out a final strategy.
"If big tobacco wants to sue for peace, we should be at the table to listen," Harshbarger said, "but we also have to be ready to try our cases. It is the cases that brought us to the talks."
